title: Chemistry detectives: how ink and flames show what things are made of

summary.text: A black sketch pen seems to hold one black ink. Put a dot of it on a paper strip and let water climb the paper. The black spreads out into other colours, such as blue, purple or yellow. Most black ink is a mixture: several dyes mixed together. The water carries each dye a different distance, so the dyes come apart. This way of separating a mixture is called chromatography. A flame can also show what is inside a thing. Salt turns a blue gas flame yellow-orange, because salt has sodium in it. Each element gives a flame its own colour. Chemists use tests like these to find out what things are made of, even the Sun.
summary.art: A paper strip hanging into a steel tumbler of water, with a black dot that has spread into blue, purple and yellow bands. Beside it, a blue gas flame flashing yellow-orange as a few grains of salt fall in.

intro.hook: Try this. Make a fat dot with a black sketch pen near the bottom of a strip of kitchen towel. Dip the very end of the strip in water, below the dot. Watch for five minutes. The water climbs, and the black dot starts to turn into other colours. Why would black ink turn into other colours?
intro.text: Chemists are scientists who find out what things are made of, and how they change. Often they cannot see the answer with their eyes alone. So they use tests that make a thing show what is in it. In this unit you use two of their oldest tests. Wet paper pulls a mixture apart. A flame shows a colour for each element. Then you use them like a detective, to find out which pen wrote a secret note.
intro.art: A child's hand dipping the end of a kitchen-towel strip into a steel tumbler of water, with a black dot just above the water line and the first blue colour creeping out of it.

outcomes: I can explain that a mixture is two or more substances mixed together, and that most black sketch pen ink is a mixture of dyes.
I can separate the dyes in a sketch pen's ink with paper and water, and explain why they come apart.
I can run a fair test to find out which pen wrote a note, and give my evidence.
I can say that each element gives a flame its own colour, and that salt turns a flame yellow-orange because it has sodium in it.
I can tell how Bunsen and Kirchhoff used the colours of flames to find new elements and to show what the Sun is made of.
I can name ways chemists' tests help people today, such as checking food, medicines and documents.

terms.meaning: A chemist is a scientist who studies what things are made of and how they change.
terms.example: A chemist in a food lab may test chilli powder to check that no extra colour was added to it.
terms.art: A woman in a lab coat holding up a paper strip with coloured bands, next to a jar of red chilli powder.

terms.meaning: A substance is one kind of material, the same all the way through. Water, salt and sugar are each a substance.
terms.example: Salt is one substance. Salt water is two substances, salt and water, mixed together.
terms.art: Three small steel bowls: one of water, one of salt, one of sugar.

terms.meaning: A mixture is two or more substances mixed together, but not joined into a new substance. A mixture can often be separated again.
terms.example: Salt water is a mixture. When the water dries up in the sun, the salt is left behind.
terms.art: A steel plate of salt water drying in the sun, with white salt crystals left around the edge.

terms.meaning: A dye is a coloured substance that dissolves in a liquid and colours what it touches.
terms.example: Sketch pen inks, food colours and the colours in a cotton saree are made with dyes.
terms.art: A row of open sketch pens, a bottle of green food colour and a folded colourful cotton saree.

terms.meaning: When a substance dissolves, it breaks up into pieces too small to see and spreads all through a liquid.
terms.example: Sugar dissolves in tea. The dyes in a sketch pen dissolve in water.
terms.art: A spoon of sugar disappearing as it is stirred into a tumbler of tea.

terms.meaning: Chromatography is a way of separating a mixture. A liquid moves through paper or powder and carries each substance a different distance. The name comes from Greek words meaning 'colour writing'.
terms.example: A dot of black sketch pen on a wet paper strip spreads into a blue band and a purple band.
terms.art: A paper strip with a black dot at the bottom and separate blue and purple bands above it.

terms.meaning: A chromatogram is the pattern of coloured bands left on the paper after chromatography.
terms.example: Your dried strip, with its bands of colour, is a chromatogram. Each ink makes its own.
terms.art: Three dried strips stuck in a notebook, each with a different pattern of bands, labelled A, B and C.

terms.meaning: Capillary action is how water creeps up through tiny gaps, such as the gaps between the fibres in paper or cloth.
terms.example: Dip one corner of a towel in a bucket of water. The wet patch slowly climbs up the towel.
terms.art: A towel hanging over the edge of a bucket, with the wet dark patch climbing up from the water.

terms.meaning: An element is a substance made of only one kind of atom. Scientists know of 118 elements.
terms.example: Sodium, copper, oxygen and carbon are elements. Salt is not an element, because it is sodium and chlorine joined together.
terms.art: Four cards labelled sodium, copper, oxygen and carbon, each with a small picture: salt, a copper wire, air bubbles and a pencil.

terms.meaning: Sodium is an element. On its own it is a soft, silvery metal, but in nature it is always joined to other elements. Table salt is sodium joined to chlorine.
terms.example: When salty rasam boils over onto a gas flame, the flame turns yellow-orange. That colour comes from sodium.
terms.art: A blue gas flame flaring yellow-orange where a little rasam has spilled over the pot's edge.

terms.meaning: A flame test finds out which elements are in a substance. You put a little of it in a flame and look at the colour.
terms.example: A flame that turns bright yellow-orange shows that there is sodium.
terms.art: A grown-up holding a wet steel spoon in the edge of a blue gas flame, which glows yellow-orange around it.

terms.meaning: Evidence is what you saw or measured that shows whether an idea is true.
terms.example: The secret note's strip had the same blue and pink bands as pen B. That is evidence that pen B wrote the note.
terms.art: A magnifying glass over two matching paper strips with the same blue and pink bands.

terms.meaning: A fair test changes only one thing and keeps everything else the same, so you know what made the difference.
terms.example: Use the same paper, the same size of dot and the same water for every pen. Only the pen changes.
terms.art: Three identical paper strips in a row, each with a dot on the same pencil line, labelled A, B and C.

terms.meaning: A forensic scientist uses science to find out what happened, often to help the police or a court.
terms.example: A forensic scientist can test the ink on a cheque to see whether someone added a word with a different pen.
terms.art: A woman scientist looking through a magnifier at handwriting on a cheque, with ink strips beside her.

explanations.definition: A pure substance is one kind of material all the way through. A mixture is two or more substances mixed together but not joined.
explanations.description: Most things around us are mixtures. Air is a mixture of gases. Seawater is water with salt and other substances dissolved in it. Rasam is water, tamarind, tomato, salt and spices. In a mixture, each substance keeps its own properties. That is why a mixture can be separated again. You only need a method that treats each substance differently. A sieve separates by size. A magnet picks out iron. Paper and water separate dyes.
examples: Muddy water: let it stand, and the mud sinks to the bottom.
Rice with small stones: people spread it on a plate and pick the stones out by hand.
Salt water: let the water dry up, and the salt is left.
explanations.art: Three ways to separate a mixture side by side: a sieve over a bowl, a magnet over a plate of iron filings and sand, and a paper strip in a tumbler with colour bands.
explanations.context: This card explains what a mixture is, and why a mixture can be separated again.

explanations.concept: Why black ink splits into colours
explanations.definition: Most black sketch pen ink is a mixture of several coloured dyes. Together they look black. Chromatography pulls them apart.
explanations.description: Mix enough colours together and your eye sees black or a very dark brown. Pen makers do this on purpose. They mix dyes such as blue, purple, red and yellow to make black. On a wet paper strip, the water climbs and dissolves the dyes in the dot. Each dye moves with the water at its own speed. So the dyes spread apart into separate bands. Different pen makers use different mixtures, so two black pens can give two different patterns.
examples: Colour one spot with every sketch pen in the box, one on top of another. You get a dark, muddy blot.
Many green sketch pens split into a yellow band and a blue band.
Some black inks are made of one black substance, such as the carbon in Indian ink. These do not split.
explanations.art: A black dot on a wet strip with arrows showing blue, purple and yellow dyes moving up the paper at different speeds.
explanations.context: This card explains why a black dot turns into other colours on wet paper.

explanations.definition: A dye that dissolves easily in water and holds on to the paper only weakly travels furthest. A dye that holds on to the paper more strongly stays nearer the dot.
explanations.description: Two things act on each dye at once. The moving water carries it up the strip. The paper fibres hold it back. Each dye is a different substance, so the balance is different for each one. Some dyes travel almost as far as the water. Others hardly leave the dot. That is what makes the pattern. With the same paper and the same liquid, the same dye always travels about the same share of the way.
examples: On kitchen towel, the blue in many black sketch pens travels further than the purple.
If the water climbs 10 cm and a dye goes 5 cm, that dye went half the way. On a longer strip, it would still go about half the way.
explanations.art: A tall strip with the water line at the top and two bands, one high and one low, with a ruler beside it.
explanations.context: This card explains why each dye stops at its own height on the strip.

explanations.concept: Some inks do not move in water
explanations.definition: Chromatography works only when the liquid can dissolve the substances. Ballpoint ink and permanent marker ink do not dissolve in water, so in water they stay on the dot.
explanations.description: Ballpoint ink is a thick paste made with oily liquids. Permanent markers use dyes that do not dissolve in water. That is why they do not wash off easily. Chemists choose a liquid that dissolves the mixture they want to test. For these inks they would use a liquid such as alcohol. A dot that does not move at all in water is still a clue. It tells you the ink is a different kind.
examples: A dot of ballpoint pen on a wet kitchen-towel strip stays a dot.
A permanent marker dot also stays where it is, while a sketch pen dot next to it spreads.
explanations.art: Two strips side by side: a sketch pen dot spread into colour bands, and a ballpoint dot still a small dark dot.
explanations.context: This card explains why some pens give no colour bands at all.

explanations.definition: Chemists use chromatography to separate and find the substances in almost any mixture, such as food, medicines, blood, water and air.
explanations.description: In a lab, the mixture is often pushed through a long, thin tube packed with powder. Each substance comes out of the far end at its own time. A machine notes when each one comes out and how much of it there is. Food labs check whether spices have added colours. Hospital labs test blood. Sports labs test for banned medicines. Forensic scientists compare the inks on documents. All of them use the same idea as your paper strip.
examples: Food safety labs in India test chilli and turmeric powder for colours that are not allowed.
A hospital lab can test a small sample of blood for many medicines at once.
explanations.art: A modern lab with a long thin coiled tube in a machine and a screen showing a line with peaks, next to a child's paper strip.
explanations.context: This card shows how the paper strip idea is used in real labs.

explanations.concept: Every element has its own flame colour
explanations.definition: When some elements are heated in a flame, they give out light of their own colour. Chemists use the colour to tell which element is there.
explanations.description: A gas stove flame is blue and almost see-through. Add a little salt, and it flashes yellow-orange. The yellow-orange comes from sodium, which is part of salt. Other elements give other colours. Copper gives green or blue. Strontium gives red. Lithium gives crimson. Potassium gives a pale lilac. Firework makers use these elements to colour their sparks. Sodium's colour is very strong. Even a tiny trace of sodium can hide the colours of the others.
examples: When rasam or dal boils over onto the stove, the blue flame flares yellow-orange for a moment.
Old orange street lights glow with the light of hot sodium.
Green fireworks usually have barium in them, and red ones strontium.
explanations.art: A row of five flames: blue gas flame, yellow-orange with sodium, green with copper, red with strontium and pale lilac with potassium.
explanations.context: This card explains why salt changes the colour of a flame, and what other colours elements make.

explanations.definition: The heat of a flame gives energy to the electrons in each atom. When the electrons give that energy out again, it comes out as light of exact colours.
explanations.description: Electrons are the tiny particles on the outside of every atom. Each kind of atom has its own set of energies that its electrons can have. So each element gives out its own exact set of colours, and no other element gives the same set. That is why a flame colour works like a fingerprint for an element. You do not need to see the atom. You only need to see its light.
examples: Sodium always gives the same yellow-orange, whether it comes from table salt, rasam or seawater.
A prism splits sodium's light into two very thin yellow lines, close together.
explanations.art: A sodium atom drawn as a small centre with electrons around it, giving out a yellow-orange ray of light.
explanations.context: This card looks inside the atom, to see where a flame's colour comes from.

explanations.concept: Reading what the Sun is made of
explanations.definition: Sunlight split into its colours has thin dark lines in it. Each element makes its own set of lines, so the lines show which elements are in the Sun.
explanations.description: Sodium gives out two thin yellow lines. Sunlight has two thin dark lines in exactly the same place. In 1859, Gustav Kirchhoff showed why. Sodium in the Sun's outer layers takes in that yellow light, so it goes missing from sunlight. Since then, astronomers have read the light of stars to find what they are made of. Most stars, like the Sun, are mostly hydrogen and helium. Helium was found in the Sun's light 27 years before anyone found it on Earth.
examples: Iron, calcium and sodium have all been found in the Sun from its light.
The Sun is about 15 crore kilometres away, and nobody has ever taken a sample of it.
explanations.art: A band of rainbow colours with thin dark lines in it, and a matching set of bright yellow lines from a salt flame below.
explanations.context: This card shows how flame colours let scientists find out what the Sun is made of.

explanations.definition: Chemists say almost nothing is perfectly pure. Nearly every substance has tiny traces of other substances in it.
explanations.description: Tap water has small amounts of dissolved salts. That is why a drop of it can make a few tiny orange flashes in a flame. Even the purest substances made in labs have a few atoms of something else. So chemists ask 'How pure is it?' rather than 'Is it pure?'. Better tests keep finding smaller and smaller traces.
examples: Bottled water lists the salts dissolved in it on the label.
A medicine packet says how pure the medicine must be.
explanations.art: A glass of tap water with a magnifier showing a few tiny dots of other substances among the water.
explanations.context: This card asks whether anything is ever made of only one substance.

agreed.text: Most coloured inks and food colours are mixtures of dyes, and chromatography can separate them.
agreed.evidence: Anyone can do it at home with paper and water. Labs separate the same dyes and name each one.

agreed.text: Each element gives out its own exact set of colours of light when it is heated.
agreed.evidence: Bunsen and Kirchhoff tested many elements in 1859 and 1860 and found each had its own pattern. Every lab since has found the same.

agreed.text: Two substances that look the same can be told apart by tests.
agreed.evidence: Salt and sugar both look like white grains. Salt turns a flame yellow-orange, and sugar melts and turns brown when heated.

agreed.text: The Sun and stars are made of the same elements as the Earth. Most stars are mostly hydrogen and helium.
agreed.evidence: The lines in starlight match the lines of elements tested in labs on Earth.

challenging.claim: Black is one colour, so black ink is one substance.
challenging.for: Black ink looks the same all over the page.
challenging.against: On wet paper, most black sketch pen inks split into several colours. Some black inks really are one substance, such as the carbon in Indian ink, and these do not split.
challenging.context: This card is about a common idea: that black ink is just black.

challenging.claim: We will never know what the stars are made of, because nobody can go there.
challenging.who: Auguste Comte, a French philosopher, in 1835
challenging.for: Nobody can travel to a star or bring back a piece of one.
challenging.against: In 1859, Kirchhoff and Bunsen showed that light carries a pattern for each element that gave it out. Starlight shows what stars are made of.
challenging.context: This card is about a famous guess that turned out wrong.

challenging.claim: A flame's colour shows only how hot it is.
challenging.for: Heat does change a flame's colour. A gas flame with plenty of air burns blue and very hot, and a candle flame is yellow and cooler.
challenging.against: What is in the flame matters too. The same blue gas flame turns yellow-orange with salt and green with copper.
challenging.context: Why are flames different colours? This card looks at a common answer that is only part of the story.

challenging.claim: Paper chromatography tells you the name of each dye.
challenging.for: Each dye makes its own band, at its own height.
challenging.against: A strip shows how many dyes there are and how far each one goes. To name a dye, chemists run a known dye beside it on the same paper, or use more tests.
challenging.context: What can a paper strip tell you, and what can't it? This card looks at a common hope.

big_questions.q: A black dot spread into blue and purple. Were the blue and purple there before, or did the water make them?
big_questions.hint: Put a blue dot and a purple dot on top of each other, and run that strip. What do you expect, and what happens?

big_questions.q: Why does each dye stop at its own height on the strip?
big_questions.hint: Think of the two things acting on each dye: the water carrying it up, and the paper holding it back.

big_questions.q: How can the light of a flame tell you what is in it, when you cannot see a single atom?
big_questions.hint: Sodium always gives the same yellow-orange. What would you need to know about other elements to use this?

big_questions.q: If two things look exactly alike, how could you ever be sure they are the same?
big_questions.hint: Think of two black pens, two white powders and two people who look alike. What tests could tell each pair apart?

big_questions.q: Your body is a mixture of thousands of substances. If a test found every one of them, would it have found you?
big_questions.hint: Is a person the substances they are made of, or something more? There is no agreed answer.

big_questions.q: We know there is sodium in the Sun without ever going there. What else could light be telling us that we have not noticed yet?
big_questions.hint: Telescopes now read the air of planets around other stars from their light.

story.title: The Extra Line on Amma's List
story.note: Kitchen-towel chromatography of sketch pens really works, and permanent marker ink really does not move in water. The family and the list are made up.
text: Every Saturday morning, Amma wrote the shopping list on the back of an old calendar page. She stuck it on the fridge with a magnet shaped like a mango. Anyone in the flat could add to it. That was the rule.
This Saturday, the list said: rice, toor dal, tomatoes, curry leaves, one coconut, soap. Then, at the very bottom, in thick black letters, someone had added: TWO BIG PACKETS OF MURUKKU.
"Who wrote this?" asked Amma. She was smiling, but only a little.

Arun, who was six, shook his head so hard that his ears went red. Revathi, who was nine, said, "Not me." Appa was reading the newspaper. He held up both hands. Ammamma, their grandmother, was out on the balcony watering her tulsi plant. She did not turn round.

Revathi looked closely at the letters. They were thick and black, like a sketch pen. "There are three black pens in this flat that could write like that," she said. "My sketch pen is in my pencil box. Arun's sketch pen is in his school bag. And there's Appa's fat black marker in the pen stand, the one he uses for parcels."
"They all look the same," said Arun. "Black is black."
"Maybe not," said Revathi. "Our science teacher showed us something. Black ink is often many colours mixed together. Amma, can I have a steel tumbler of water and the kitchen towel?"

She cut three long strips of kitchen towel. Near the bottom of each one, she drew a pencil line. On each line she made a fat black dot, one dot from each pen. At the top she wrote R, A and P in pencil, for Revathi, Arun and Appa. Amma, who was the judge, cut a thin strip off the bottom of the list. It went right through the tail of the letter S in PACKETS.

Revathi laid a pencil across the top of the tumbler. She hung all four strips over it, so that their ends just touched the water. The dots stayed above the water. Arun lay on the floor with his chin in his hands and watched.

The water crept up the towel. When it reached the dots, the black began to run. On strip R, the black spread into a blue band, with a purple band above it. On strip A, it became blue at the bottom and pink higher up. On strip P, the black did not move at all. It stayed a dark, sharp dot.
"Appa's marker is a different kind of ink," said Revathi. "Water can't dissolve it, so water can't carry it."

The strip from the list was slower, because calendar paper is thicker than kitchen towel. They waited. Appa put down his newspaper and came to watch too. At last a blue smudge crept out of the letter. Above it, faint but clear, came a pink one.
"Blue and pink," said Revathi. "The same as strip A." Everyone looked at Arun.
Arun went red again. "But I didn't! I can't even write murukku!" That was true. He could write his own name, and CAT, and that was all.
Revathi frowned at the strips. Then she said slowly, "The strip tells us which pen. It doesn't tell us whose hand. Arun, who else used your sketch pen this week?"
Arun thought hard. "Ammamma borrowed it. On Thursday. To write the label on her mango pickle jar."
Everyone turned to the balcony. Ammamma put down her watering can. She came inside slowly, with a very straight face. "A list is for the things a house needs," she said. "This house needs murukku."

Amma laughed so much she had to sit down. Appa said Ammamma was clearly a very clever criminal. Ammamma said she was seventy-two, far too old to be a criminal, and she would like her murukku now, please.

Later, Revathi stuck the four dried strips into her notebook in a row. Under them she wrote: All three pens looked black. Inside, they were different. The strip tells you which pen, not who held it. So you have to ask more questions.

That evening, Arun took his sketch pen and made a careful dot on a strip of towel, all by himself. He watched the blue and the pink creep apart. "So the blue and the pink were in there all the time," he said. "Yes," said Revathi. "Black is how they look when they are together."
story.epiphany: For the parent: two black inks can look the same on paper but be made of different dyes. Water carries each dye its own distance, so each ink leaves its own pattern, its chromatogram. The strip from the list matched pen A, so pen A wrote it. Appa's marker did not move, because permanent marker ink does not dissolve in water. Revathi also sees the limit of her evidence. The test answers 'which pen?', not 'who?'. Real forensic scientists say the same: a test answers one question, and the rest needs more questions.
ask: Why did Revathi make a separate strip for each pen?
Why did the black from Appa's parcel marker stay as a dot?
The list matched Arun's pen. Why did Revathi not decide that Arun wrote it?
What could Revathi do if two pens gave exactly the same pattern?

check.q: A friend says a dot of black sketch pen will stay black on wet paper. What is most likely to happen?
options: It spreads into two or more colours
check.why: Most black sketch pen ink is a mixture of dyes. The water carries each dye a different distance, so the colours come apart. Picking 'stays black' means thinking black is one substance. Picking 'disappears' means forgetting that the dyes stay on the paper.

games.title: Secret Mix: guess the pens from the bands
games.context: In this game one player secretly mixes two sketch pen colours in one dot. The other player runs the strip and works out which two pens were used.

printables.title: Secret Mix score sheet

rules: Pick 4 sketch pen colours that look different, for example yellow, blue, pink and green.
The mixer turns away and puts two dots on top of each other on a strip's pencil line, one from each of two pens. They write the two colours on the score sheet and fold it over.
The guesser runs the strip in water and watches the bands.
The guesser says which two pens were used, and why.

flow.do: 1. Cut 6 strips of kitchen towel, 2 cm wide and 12 cm long. 2. Draw a pencil line 2 cm from the bottom of each. 3. On one test strip, make one dot of each of the 4 pens, side by side.
flow.say: First let's see what each pen does alone. Then we'll know what to look for.
flow.kid: Make a test strip with one dot of each pen. Run it in water.

flow.do: Play the rounds. Run each secret strip in a tumbler with 1 cm of water, until the water is near the top.
flow.say: Look at the bands. Which pens' colours can you see? How do you know?
flow.kid: Watch your strip. Which colours came out? Which pens made them?
flow.parent: Green often splits into yellow and blue. So a green and yellow mix can look like green alone. That is a real puzzle, so let your child argue it out. Leave each strip in the water about 5 to 8 minutes.

flow.say: Which mix was hardest to guess? Why was it hard?
flow.kid: Which mix was hardest? Why?

check.q: A secret strip shows a yellow band and a blue band. Which mix could it be?
options: Yellow and blue, or a green that splits into yellow and blue
check.why: Many green sketch pens are a mixture of yellow and blue dyes. So the same bands could come from a yellow and a blue pen, or from a green pen. Picking 'only yellow and blue' forgets that green can be a mixture. Pink and green would give a pink band too.

experiments.title: Which Pen Wrote the Note?
experiments.context: In this experiment a grown-up writes a secret letter with one of three dark pens. You make a strip for each pen and let water climb them. Then you match the secret letter's colours to find the pen.
experiments.question: Three dark pens look almost the same. Can water and paper show which one wrote a secret letter?
experiments.predict: Look at the three pens' marks on paper. Do you think their inks are the same? What do you think each ink will do when the water reaches it? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same kind of strip for every pen. Draw every dot on a pencil line 2 cm from the bottom, the same size, gone over 3 times. Dip every strip 1 cm into the same water, for the same time. Only the pen changes.
results_table: My guess: what will the ink do?
Colours I saw, from bottom to top
Does it match the secret letter?

materials.item: 3 dark pens that look alike: black sketch pens from two different packets or makers, and one more dark pen, such as another black sketch pen, a dark brown or dark blue sketch pen, or a black permanent marker
strips of white kitchen towel, about 2 cm wide and 12 cm long. Blotting paper from a stationery shop works even better. A thick white paper napkin, folded double, also works.
two steel tumblers or glasses, with water 1 cm deep
a pencil, a ruler and scissors
two clothes clips, or sticky tape
a plate, to dry the strips on

experiments.safety: A grown-up helps with the scissors. Wipe up spilled water so nobody slips.

schedule.what: A grown-up writes a secret letter with one pen. Make a strip for each pen. Run all four strips in water, dry them and match the secret letter.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Stick the dried strips into your notebook in a row, and write under them which pen wrote the secret letter and how you know.

flow.do: 1. Lay the three pens on the table. Call them A, B and C. 2. Scribble a little with each on scrap paper. 3. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: These three inks all look dark. Do you think they are the same ink? What will each one do when water reaches it? Why?
flow.kid: Look at the three scribbles. Are the inks the same? Guess what water will do. Why?

ask.q: What do you think will happen to the black dot?
good: It might turn into other colours, like the intro strip.

flow.parent: Write down your child's guess and their reason in the table before testing. Any guess is fine. The test decides.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Which Pen test. You look at three dark pens and guess what water will do to each ink.

flow.do: 1. The child turns away. 2. The grown-up picks one pen secretly. 3. On a fourth strip, they draw a pencil line 2 cm from the bottom. 4. They write one thick letter, such as P, sitting on the line. 5. They mark a star at the top and hide the pen.
flow.say: No peeking. I'm writing a secret letter with one of the three pens. Your job is to find out which.
flow.kid: Turn away. A grown-up is writing a secret letter. Which pen? You will find out!
flow.parent: Go over the letter twice, so there is plenty of ink. Keep it small, about 1 cm tall, and on the line. Put the pens back in a row so the child can't tell which one you used.

flow.do: 1. Draw a pencil line 2 cm from the bottom of three strips. 2. Write A, B and C at the top in pencil. 3. On each line, make a dot as wide as a pencil with its pen. 4. Let it dry for a few seconds, then go over it twice more.
flow.say: We use pencil for the line and the labels, because pencil does not dissolve in water. A small, strong dot gives the clearest bands.
flow.kid: Draw a pencil line on each strip. Write A, B, C on top. Make a small, dark dot on each line.
flow.parent: A dot about 4 to 5 mm across works best. A big blot smears the bands together.

flow.do: 1. Pour water 1 cm deep into each tumbler. 2. Clip two strips to a pencil, and lay it across one tumbler. 3. Do the same with the other two strips. 4. Check that each strip's end is in the water and each dot is above it.
flow.say: The dot must stay above the water. If it goes under, the ink just washes into the tumbler. Why do you think the strips must not touch?
flow.kid: Clip the strips to a pencil. Lay it on the tumbler. The dot stays above the water!
flow.parent: Strips must not touch each other or the sides of the tumbler, or the colours will run across. If the water is too deep, pour a little out.

flow.do: 1. Watch the water climb. 2. When the water reaches about 1 cm from the top, lift the strips out. 3. Mark with pencil how high the water reached on each strip.
flow.say: Watch the dots. What is happening to the ink? Which strip is changing first?
flow.kid: Watch the water climb. What happens when it reaches the dots?

ask.q: What do you see on each strip?
good: The black is spreading into blue and purple.
One strip has pink in it and the others don't.
One dot is not moving at all.

flow.parent: On kitchen towel, the water climbs about 8 to 10 cm in 5 to 10 minutes. Blotting paper is slower. A permanent marker dot will not move, which is a useful result. If every black dot stays black, try a different black sketch pen, or a dark brown or purple one.

flow.do: 1. Lay the strips flat on a plate to dry. 2. For each strip, write the colours from bottom to top in the table. 3. Measure from the pencil line to the top of the highest colour.
flow.say: Let's record what each ink became. Which colours, in which order, and how high?
flow.kid: Lay the strips on a plate. Write each strip's colours, bottom to top. Measure the top colour.
flow.parent: Colours fade a little as they dry, so write them down while the strips are still damp.

flow.do: 1. Put the star strip next to strips A, B and C. 2. Find the one with the same colours in the same order. 3. Ask your child to say what they think, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: Which strip matches the secret letter? What is your evidence? Tell me what you think, what you saw, and why.
flow.kid: Put the star strip next to A, B and C. Which one matches? Say what you think, what you saw, and why.

check.q: The secret letter's strip shows a blue band low down and a pink band higher up. Strip A shows blue and purple. Strip B shows blue low down and pink higher up. Strip C did not move. Which pen wrote the letter?
check.why: Pen B's ink split into the same colours, in the same order, as the secret letter. Pen A has purple, not pink. Pen C did not move at all, but the letter's ink did. A strong answer names the colours and their order as evidence.

flow.parent: A good answer: What I think: pen B wrote it. What I saw: the star strip and strip B both had blue at the bottom and pink above it. Why: each ink is its own mix of dyes, so it makes its own pattern.

flow.do: The grown-up shows which pen they used.
flow.say: Let's check. Were you right?
flow.kid: Now the grown-up shows the pen. Were you right?
flow.think: If two of the pens had given exactly the same pattern, how could you tell them apart?

setup.caption: 1. Dot each pen on its own strip. A grown-up writes the secret letter.

experiments.title: Does Every Colour Split?
experiments.context: In this experiment you test six sketch pen colours. You find out which inks are one dye and which are mixtures of dyes.
experiments.question: Which sketch pen colours are one dye, and which are mixtures of two or more dyes?
experiments.predict: Look at six sketch pens. Which colours do you think will stay one colour, and which will split? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same kind of strip and the same size of dot for every pen. Draw every dot on a pencil line 2 cm from the bottom. Dip every strip 1 cm into water and take them all out at the same time.
results_table: My guess: one dye or a mixture?
Colours I saw, from bottom to top

materials.item: 6 sketch pens of different colours, for example black, brown, green, purple, orange and yellow
strips of white kitchen towel, about 2 cm wide and 12 cm long. Blotting paper from a stationery shop works even better. A thick white paper napkin, folded double, also works.
three steel tumblers or glasses, with water 1 cm deep
a pencil, a ruler, scissors and three clothes clips or tape

experiments.safety: A grown-up helps with the scissors.

schedule.what: Make a strip for each of six colours. Run them two to a tumbler. Count the dyes in each.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw a bar chart of how many dyes each colour had.

flow.do: 1. Lay out the six pens. 2. Ask your child to sort them into 'one dye' and 'a mixture'.
flow.say: Which of these colours do you think are made of just one dye? Which might be a mix? Why?
flow.kid: Sort the pens. One dye, or a mix? Why do you think so?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Does Every Colour Split test. You guess which pen colours are mixtures.

flow.do: 1. Make a strip for each pen, with a pencil line 2 cm from the bottom and a small, dark dot on it. 2. Write the colour at the top in pencil. 3. Clip two strips to each pencil and lay them across three tumblers.
flow.say: Same paper, same size of dot, same water. Only the colour of the pen changes.
flow.kid: Make a strip for each pen. Hang two strips in each tumbler.

flow.do: Wait until the water is about 1 cm from the top of the strips. Then lift them all out together and lay them flat.
flow.say: Which colours are splitting? Which are staying together?
flow.kid: Watch. Which colours split? Which stay as one?
flow.parent: Results depend on the maker. Often yellow and blue stay as one dye. Green often splits into yellow and blue, and brown and black into three or more.

flow.do: 1. Count the separate colours on each strip. 2. Fill in the table. 3. Ask the question below.
flow.say: How many dyes were in each pen? Which surprised you?
flow.kid: Count the colours on each strip. Which one surprised you?

check.q: A green sketch pen splits into a yellow band and a blue band. What does that tell you?
options: The water turned the green into yellow and blue
The green ink is a mixture of a yellow dye and a blue dye
check.why: The yellow and blue dyes were in the ink all along. Mixed together, they look green. The water only carried them different distances, so they came apart. Picking 'the water turned it' is a natural first idea. To test it, run a strip of a yellow pen and a blue pen dotted together, and see if it looks like the green one.

setup.caption: 1. One dot of each colour on its own strip.

setup.caption: 2. Hang two strips in each tumbler.

experiments.title: The Flame Test: which cup has salt in it?
experiments.context: In this experiment a grown-up holds a wet steel spoon in a gas flame. Three cups of water look the same, but one has salt in it. You use the flame's colour to find it.
experiments.question: Three cups of water look the same. Can a flame show which one has salt dissolved in it?
experiments.predict: One cup is plain water, one is sugar water and one is salt water. They all look clear. What do you think the flame will do with each one? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same amount of liquid on the same kind of spoon. The grown-up holds each spoon in the same part of the flame for the same time, 5 seconds. Only the liquid changes.
results_table: My guess: what is in it?
What I now think is in it

materials.item: a gas stove, used only by a grown-up
three small steel cups or katoris, labelled 1, 2 and 3 underneath by a grown-up
half a teaspoon of salt and half a teaspoon of sugar
three clean, dry steel spoons
a cloth to hold the spoons, and the sink to cool them in

experiments.safety: Only a grown-up lights the stove and holds the spoons in the flame. The child stands at least one metre away. Tie back long hair, and keep dupattas and loose sleeves away from the stove. The spoon gets hot: cool it in the sink. Homes with induction cooktops have no flame. Instead, watch the coloured flames video in this unit.

schedule.what: A grown-up makes salt water, sugar water and plain water in three secret cups. Hold a wet spoon from each in the gas flame. Use the colours to find the salt.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the flame for each cup, with the colour you saw.

flow.do: 1. The child turns away. 2. The grown-up stirs half a teaspoon of salt into one cup of water, and half a teaspoon of sugar into another. 3. The third cup is plain water. 4. Write 1, 2 and 3 on paper under the cups, and note secretly which is which.
flow.say: These three cups look the same. One has salt in it, one has sugar, and one is plain water. Can a flame tell them apart? What do you think, and why?
flow.kid: Three cups look the same. One has salt. Guess: can a flame find it? Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of the flame test. A grown-up makes three cups of water that look the same.

flow.do: 1. The child stands at least one metre from the stove. 2. The grown-up lights one burner on low. 3. Look at the flame's colour before testing anything.
flow.say: Look at the flame first. What colour is it? We need to know that before we test anything.
flow.kid: Stand back one big step. Look at the flame. What colour is it?
flow.parent: A gas flame is mostly blue. Remember this colour, because it is the 'before' for every test.

flow.do: 1. Dip the bowl of spoon 1 into cup 1. 2. Hold the wet spoon in the edge of the flame for 5 seconds. 3. Watch the colour. 4. Cool the spoon in the sink. 5. Do the same for cups 2 and 3, with a clean spoon each time.
flow.say: Watch the edge of the flame around the spoon. What colour do you see? Does it last?
flow.kid: Watch the flame by the spoon. What colour? Does it last?
flow.parent: The salt water gives bright yellow-orange flashes that keep coming as the water boils off. Plain tap water may give a few tiny orange sparks, because tap water has a little salt in it too. Sugar water gives little or no colour. Hold the spoon by its end with a cloth. Never hold your face over the flame.

flow.do: 1. Fill in the table. 2. Ask your child to say which cup has salt, and why. 3. Uncover the secret labels.
flow.say: Which cup has salt in it? What did you see that tells you? Now let's check the labels.
flow.kid: Which cup had salt? What is your evidence? Check the labels.

check.q: Cup 2 made the flame flash bright yellow-orange. Cups 1 and 3 hardly changed the flame. What is in cup 2?
check.why: Salt is sodium joined to chlorine. Sodium in a flame gives out bright yellow-orange light, so the salty cup is the one that flashed. Sugar has no sodium, so it gives little colour. A strong answer says that the colour comes from sodium.

flow.do: Turn off the stove. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Salt water and sugar water look exactly the same. So how did the flame tell them apart?
flow.kid: The cups looked the same. How did the flame tell them apart?
flow.think: When rasam boils over onto the stove, the flame turns yellow-orange. What is in rasam that does that?

activities.title: One Dot, Five Minutes
activities.context: A quick first look. You put one black dot on a strip and watch what water does to it, before learning anything about it.

materials.item: one black sketch pen
one strip of kitchen towel, about 2 cm wide and 12 cm long
a steel tumbler with water 1 cm deep, and a pencil

schedule.what: Put a black dot on a kitchen-towel strip and watch what happens when water climbs it.

activities.record: Draw the strip before and after.

flow.do: 1. Make a fat black dot 2 cm from the bottom of the strip. 2. Ask the question below.
flow.say: What do you think will happen to this dot when the water reaches it? Why?
flow.kid: Make a black dot near the bottom. What will water do to it? Why?
flow.context: This is a quick first look at what water does to a black ink dot.

flow.do: 1. Hang the strip over the edge of the tumbler, so the end dips in the water and the dot stays above it. 2. Watch for five minutes.
flow.say: Just watch. What do you notice? What do you wonder?
flow.kid: Hang the strip in the water. Watch the dot. What do you see?

ask.q: What do you notice? What do you wonder?
good: Colours are coming out of the black.
Where did the colours come from?

flow.do: Lift the strip out and lay it on a plate.
flow.say: Keep that question in your head. The Which Pen test will help us answer it.
flow.kid: Lift it out. Keep your question. We will answer it soon.

check.q: Which of these is the best question to ask next?
options: Was the colour already in the black ink?
check.why: This question can be tested: try other black pens, or mix two colours on one dot and see if they come apart too. The other two questions are much harder to test.

setup.caption: 1. Make one black dot near the bottom.

setup.caption: 2. Dip the end in water and watch.

activities.title: Chalk Column, Like Tsvet
activities.context: In 1903, Mikhail Tsvet separated the coloured substances in leaves by pouring them through a glass tube packed with chalk powder. In this activity you separate sketch pen ink on a stick of white chalk.

materials.item: a stick of white blackboard chalk
2 or 3 sketch pens: black, brown or green work best
a steel bowl or small plate with water about half a centimetre deep

schedule.what: Draw an ink ring round a stick of chalk, stand it in shallow water, and watch the dyes climb and separate.

activities.record: Draw the chalk stick with its colour bands. Compare it with a paper strip of the same pen.

flow.do: 1. Draw a thick ring all the way round the chalk, about 1.5 cm from the bottom, with a sketch pen. 2. Go round it twice.
flow.say: Chalk is a powder pressed into a stick. Tsvet used a tube of chalk powder to separate the colours in leaves.
flow.kid: Draw a thick ring round the chalk, near the bottom. Go round twice.
flow.context: This is the first step of the chalk column. You draw an ink ring round a stick of chalk.

flow.do: 1. Stand the chalk upright in the shallow water, ring end down. 2. Make sure the ring is above the water. 3. Watch for about 10 minutes, until the water is near the top.
flow.say: Watch the ring. Do the colours move the same way as on the paper strip?
flow.kid: Stand the chalk in the water. The ring stays above the water. Watch.
flow.parent: Water climbs chalk quickly. The colours usually spread into bands, like on paper, but they may go to different heights. If the chalk falls over, lean it against the side of the bowl.

flow.do: Lift the chalk out and let it dry. Compare it with a paper strip of the same pen.
flow.say: Are the bands in the same order as on paper? What does that tell you about the chalk?
flow.kid: Let it dry. Are the colours in the same order as on paper?

check.q: Tsvet poured leaf colour through a tube of chalk powder, and it came apart into green and yellow bands. Why did it come apart?
options: Each coloured substance moved through the chalk at its own speed
check.why: The leaf colour was a mixture. As the liquid ran through the chalk, each substance moved at its own speed, so they spread into bands. It is the same idea as your paper strip. The chalk does not add colour: try a plain chalk stick in water, and it stays white.

activities.title: Ink Flowers for a Festival Card
activities.context: In this art activity you drip water onto a ring of sketch pen dots on a paper circle. The dyes spread outwards into rings of colour, and you make the circle into a flower for a Pongal, Onam or Deepavali card.

materials.item: a circle of kitchen towel or a white paper napkin, about 12 cm across
sketch pens of several colours
a steel tumbler, a teaspoon and a little water
a piece of card, glue and a green sketch pen for the stem

schedule.what: Make ink rings on paper circles, drip water in the middle, dry them and make flowers for a card.

activities.record: Stick your best flower on a card. Under it, write which pens split into the most colours.

flow.do: 1. Draw a ring of dots round the centre of a paper circle, about 2 cm from the middle. 2. Use different colours for the dots.
flow.say: Which colours do you think will spread the most? Let's see.
flow.kid: Draw a ring of dots round the middle of the circle.
flow.context: This is the first step of the ink flower art. You draw a ring of dots on a paper circle.

flow.do: 1. Lay the circle flat on top of the empty tumbler. 2. Drip water onto the very centre, a few drops at a time, from a teaspoon. 3. Stop when the colours are near the edge.
flow.say: Slowly, a few drops at a time. Watch the colours race outwards.
flow.kid: Put the circle on the tumbler. Drip water in the middle, slowly. Watch.
flow.parent: Too much water at once makes the colours run together into a puddle. Five or six teaspoons over a few minutes is usually enough.

flow.do: 1. Lay the circles on a plate to dry. 2. Pinch each circle in the middle and twist it into a flower. 3. Glue it on the card and draw a stem.
flow.say: Look at the rings. Which pen made the most colours? Which made only one?
flow.kid: Dry the circles. Pinch and twist into a flower. Glue it on a card.

ask.q: Why did the colours make rings this time, not bands?
good: Because the water spread out from the middle in every direction.
The dyes went outwards instead of upwards.

activities.title: Three White Powders: a detective's tests
activities.context: Salt, sugar and cooking soda all look like white powder. In this activity you use three tests to tell them apart, then find out what a mystery powder is.

materials.item: half a teaspoon each of salt, sugar and cooking soda, on three small plates labelled in pencil
a fourth plate with a mystery powder: one of the three, chosen secretly by a grown-up
a few spoons of water and a little lemon juice
a magnifying glass, if you have one
a steel spoon and a gas stove, used only by a grown-up

activities.safety: Do not taste the powders. A grown-up does the heating, and the child stands at least one metre from the stove. The spoon gets very hot: cool it in the sink.

schedule.what: Look closely at three white powders, add lemon juice, and heat them. Use the results to name a mystery powder.

activities.record: Make a table with the three powders down the side and the three tests along the top. Write what each powder did.

flow.do: 1. Look at each powder closely, with a magnifier if you have one. 2. Describe the grains.
flow.say: All three look white. What differences can you see when you look really closely?
flow.kid: Look closely at each powder. What do the grains look like?
flow.parent: Salt grains are often small cubes. Sugar grains are a little bigger and shinier. Cooking soda is a fine, soft powder.
flow.context: This is the first step of the three white powders test. You look closely at salt, sugar and cooking soda.

flow.do: 1. Put a pinch of each powder in its own spoon. 2. Add a few drops of lemon juice to each. 3. Watch for bubbles.
flow.say: Lemon juice is an acid. Watch closely. Does anything fizz?
flow.kid: Add lemon juice to each powder. Which one fizzes?
flow.parent: Only the cooking soda fizzes. It makes a gas called carbon dioxide.

flow.do: 1. The child stands back. 2. The grown-up heats a pinch of each powder on a steel spoon over a low flame. 3. Each one gets about 20 seconds. 4. Watch and listen.
flow.say: Watch from back here. What happens to each powder when it is heated?
flow.kid: Stand back. Watch each powder heat up. What happens?
flow.parent: Sugar melts and turns brown, then black, and smells of caramel. Salt does not melt on a stove. It may crackle, and the flame near the spoon may flash yellow-orange. Cooking soda does not melt either. It has sodium in it too, so the flame may flash yellow-orange near it as well. Wash the spoon after each powder.

flow.do: 1. The grown-up gives the mystery plate. 2. The child chooses which tests to do. 3. They name the powder and give their evidence.
flow.say: Here is the mystery powder. Which tests will you use? What is it, and how do you know?
flow.kid: Test the mystery powder. What is it? How do you know?

check.q: The mystery powder does not fizz with lemon juice. When it is heated, it melts and turns brown. What is it?
check.why: Cooking soda would have fizzed. Salt does not melt on a stove. Only sugar melts and turns brown. A strong answer uses two tests, because two pieces of evidence are stronger than one.

activities.title: Flame Colour Spotter
activities.context: Coloured flames and lights show up in daily life. For one week, you spot them and work out which element made each colour.

materials.item: a notebook and a pencil

activities.safety: Only look at flames from a safe distance. Watch fireworks only with a grown-up, from far away.

schedule.what: Make a spotter page with columns: where, colour, which element.
Look back at your page. Which colour did you spot most often?

activities.record: A page with three columns: where I saw it, what colour, which element I think made it.

flow.do: Help your child make a spotter page with three columns: where, colour, element.
flow.say: This week, let's look out for coloured flames and lights. Watch the stove when milk or rasam boils over. Look at old orange street lights.
flow.kid: Make a page. Where? What colour? Which element? Look all week.
flow.context: This is a week-long spotting activity. You look for coloured flames and lights and guess which element made them.

flow.do: On day 7, read the page together.
flow.say: Which colour did you see most? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at your page. Which colour did you see most?
flow.parent: Yellow-orange from sodium is by far the most common, because salt is everywhere: in food, sweat and tap water. Old orange street lights use sodium too. If you see fireworks at Deepavali, red is usually strontium, green is barium and blue is copper.

check.q: Milk boils over onto the gas flame, and it flashes yellow-orange. Milk has a little salt in it. Which element made the colour?
check.why: Milk has small amounts of salt in it, and salt has sodium. Sodium makes a flame yellow-orange. Copper would give green or blue.

projects.title: Our Home Ink Library
projects.context: Chemists keep libraries of known substances to compare unknown ones with. In this project you make a library of every pen in your home, then use it to solve a family mystery.

materials.item: every pen and marker you can find at home: sketch pens, felt pens, highlighters, ballpoint pens, gel pens, a whiteboard marker
strips of kitchen towel or blotting paper, one for each pen
two or three steel tumblers with water 1 cm deep, a pencil and clothes clips
a big sheet of paper and glue

projects.safety: A grown-up helps with the scissors.

schedule.what: Make a strip for every pen at home, run them and stick them on a chart with labels.
A family member writes a secret word with one pen. Run it and find the pen using your library.

projects.record: The library chart: each strip, the pen's name, and 'moves' or 'does not move'. Then the solved mystery, with your evidence.

flow.do: 1. Make a strip for each pen, labelled in pencil. 2. Run them in water, two or three at a time. 3. Dry them and glue them on the chart in a row. 4. Under each, write the pen's name and what it did.
flow.say: Let's make a library of every ink in the house. Later, we can compare any mystery ink with it.
flow.kid: Make a strip for every pen. Run them. Stick them on a chart with names.
flow.parent: Ballpoint pens, gel pens and permanent markers often do not move in water. Write 'does not move' for those. It is still useful information.
flow.context: This is day 1 of the ink library. You make a strip for every pen at home and stick them on a chart.

flow.do: 1. A family member writes one short word on a strip's pencil line, with any pen from the library. 2. The child runs it. 3. They compare it with the chart and name the pen.
flow.say: Here's a mystery word. Use your library to find the pen. What is your evidence?
flow.kid: Run the mystery word. Compare it with your chart. Which pen?

check.q: The mystery word did not move in water at all. What can you tell from that?
options: It was written with an ink that does not dissolve in water, such as a ballpoint or permanent marker
It was written with a sketch pen
check.why: Sketch pen inks dissolve in water and move. An ink that stays put does not dissolve in water. This narrows it down to the pens marked 'does not move' in your library. A chemist would then test those with a different liquid.

challenges.title: The Sharpest Bands
challenges.problem: On your first strips, the bands may have been blurry and close together. Find a way to make the colours of one black pen come apart further and more sharply.
constraints: Use the same black pen for every try.
Keep your first strip, so you can compare.
materials: kitchen towel, blotting paper, paper napkins, newspaper edge, white chalk
steel tumblers, water, a pinch of salt
a ruler, a pencil and clothes clips
general: Make the dot smaller and darker: a tiny dot, gone over several times, gives sharper bands.
Use a longer strip, so the dyes have further to travel and spread out more.
Try blotting paper, which is thicker and more even than kitchen towel.
creative: Let the first run dry, turn the strip sideways and run it again in a second direction. Chemists do this to separate dyes that sit too close together.
Add a pinch of salt to the water and compare. A different liquid can change how far each dye travels.
Use a stick of chalk instead of paper, like Mikhail Tsvet's chalk column.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own way. Change only one thing at a time, run the strip, and compare it with your first one. Which change made the biggest difference?

flow.do: 1. Look at a strip from the Which Pen test. 2. Find the bands that are blurry or too close together.
flow.say: Engineers start by looking at the problem closely. Where are the colours running into each other?
flow.kid: Look at your old strip. Which colours are blurry or squashed together?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Sharpest Bands challenge. You look at what went wrong with your first strips.

flow.do: Draw three ideas before trying any.
flow.say: Let's think of three changes. Remember, change only one thing at a time, or we won't know which one worked.
flow.kid: Draw three ideas. Change only one thing each time.

flow.do: 1. Try each idea with a new strip. 2. Measure the gap between the bands. 3. Compare with the first strip.
flow.say: Which change spread the colours furthest apart? How do you know?
flow.kid: Try each idea. Measure the gap between colours. Which is best?

flow.do: Ask the question below.
flow.say: Why do you think that change worked best?
flow.kid: Which idea worked best? Why?

check.q: Meena, a girl in Class 3, made her strip twice as long, and her bands spread further apart. Why?
options: The dyes had further to travel, so the faster ones got further ahead
Longer paper has more dye in it
check.why: Each dye travels about the same share of the way. On a longer strip, the gap between a fast dye and a slow one grows too. Picking 'more dye in it' forgets that all the dye comes from the dot.
