quiz.p: Salt water is made of salt and water mixed together. What kind of material is it?
quiz.why: Salt water is two substances mixed but not joined, so it is a mixture. When the water dries up, the salt is left behind. Picking 'element' means mixing up an element, one kind of atom, with any material.

quiz.p: A black sketch pen dot on a wet paper strip spreads into blue and purple bands. Where did the blue and purple come from?
opts: They were in the black ink all along
The paper had them in it
quiz.why: The black ink is a mixture of blue and purple dyes. The water only carried them different distances, so they came apart. A plain wet strip with no dot stays white, so the paper and water did not make them.

quiz.p: Why must the ink dot stay above the water when you start?
opts: So the ink does not just wash off into the tumbler
So the paper does not tear
quiz.why: If the dot is under the water, the dyes dissolve into the water in the tumbler instead of climbing the strip. Above the water, the climbing water carries them up the paper.

quiz.p: On a strip, the blue dye went 8 cm and the purple dye went 4 cm. Why did the blue go further?
opts: The blue dye holds on to the paper less strongly than the purple
There was more blue in the dot
quiz.why: The water carries each dye up, and the paper holds each dye back. A dye that holds the paper less strongly travels further. Picking 'more blue' is a natural guess, but a bigger amount gives a darker band, not a longer trip.

quiz.p: Why do we draw the start line on the strip in pencil, not in pen?
opts: Pencil is easier to rub out
Pencil does not dissolve in water, so it will not run
quiz.why: Pencil marks are made of graphite, which does not dissolve in water. A pen line could dissolve and run up the strip, mixing with the colours you are testing.

quiz.p: Kavya, a girl in Class 3, tests three pens. She uses kitchen towel for pen A, blotting paper for pen B and newspaper for pen C. Why is this not a fair test?
opts: She changed the paper as well as the pen
She should have used ink, not pens
quiz.why: In a fair test only one thing changes. Kavya changed the pen and the paper, so she cannot tell whether a difference came from the ink or from the paper.

quiz.p: The secret note's strip has the same colours, in the same order, as pen B's strip. What does that show?
opts: Pen B's ink is the same mixture as the note's ink
Pen B's owner wrote the note
All the pens are the same
quiz.why: The strip shows which ink, so it points to pen B. It does not show whose hand held pen B. That needs more questions, as Revathi found in the story.

quiz.p: A grown-up holds a spoon of salt water in a gas flame. What colour does the flame turn?
quiz.why: Salt has sodium in it, and sodium makes a flame yellow-orange. Green would mean copper or barium, and red would mean strontium or lithium.

quiz.p: Firework makers want a red firework. Which element should they add?
quiz.why: Strontium gives a bright red. Sodium gives yellow-orange and copper gives green or blue. Each element gives its own colours, and that is how fireworks get theirs.

quiz.p: In 1835, Auguste Comte said we would never know what stars are made of. How were Bunsen and Kirchhoff able to show he was wrong?
opts: They found that each element's light has its own pattern, and matched sodium's pattern in sunlight
They dug up a fallen star
quiz.why: Kirchhoff and Bunsen found that each element gives out its own set of colours. Sodium's yellow matched two dark lines in sunlight, which showed sodium is in the Sun. Nobody had to go there.

quiz.p: Bunsen and Kirchhoff found a new element in spring water because of a colour no known element gave. What colour was it?
opts: Sky blue, so they named it caesium
Bright green, so they named it chlorine
Yellow, so they named it sodium
quiz.why: In 1860 they saw blue lines that no known element made. They named the new element caesium, from a Latin word for sky blue. A year later, red lines led them to rubidium.

quiz.p: A food safety lab wants to check whether some chilli powder has a colour added that is not allowed. Which method would help most?
opts: Separate the colours in it, like chromatography
quiz.why: Chromatography separates the coloured substances in the powder, so the lab can see whether there is a dye that should not be there. Weighing or smelling cannot show which colours are mixed in.

items.p: Lakshmi, a girl in Class 3 in Kochi, looks at things in her kitchen. Sort each one: is it a mixture or a pure substance?
items: distilled water, the kind sold for batteries
items.a: see items
items.why: A mixture has two or more substances mixed together. Rasam, air, ink, muddy water and salt water are mixtures. Sugar, salt and distilled water are each one substance, almost pure. A strong answer can say what is mixed in each mixture.

items.p: A pure substance, such as sugar, can be separated into different colours with paper and water.
items.why: False. Paper and water separate a mixture into the substances in it. A pure substance has only one substance to start with, so there is nothing to separate.

items.p: Separating a mixture of dyes by letting a liquid climb paper is called ____.
a: chromatography
items.why: The word comes from Greek words meaning 'colour writing', because the first separations were of coloured substances.

items.p: When you dip the end of a kitchen-towel strip in water, the water climbs up it. What makes it climb?
opts: Capillary action: water creeping through the tiny gaps between the paper's fibres
The ink pulls the water up
items.why: Paper is made of tiny fibres with tiny gaps between them. Water creeps up through the gaps. This is capillary action. A plain strip with no ink climbs just as well, so the ink is not pulling it.

items.p: Put the steps of the Which Pen test in order.
items: Hang the strips so their ends dip in the water
Draw a pencil line 2 cm from the bottom of each strip
Compare the dried strips with the secret letter's strip
Make a dot of ink on each pencil line
Wait until the water is near the top, then take the strips out
a: Draw a pencil line 2 cm from the bottom of each strip
Make a dot of ink on each pencil line
Hang the strips so their ends dip in the water
Wait until the water is near the top, then take the strips out
Compare the dried strips with the secret letter's strip
items.why: First mark where the dot goes, then put the ink on, then let the water carry the dyes, and only then compare the patterns.

items.p: Here is a drawing of one strip hanging in a tumbler during the Which Pen test. Label the parts.
a: The clip is at the top, holding the strip to the pencil.
The paper strip hangs down into the tumbler.
The pencil line is 2 cm from the bottom of the strip.
The ink dot sits on the pencil line.
The water is at the bottom, below the dot.
items.why: A strong answer puts the ink dot above the water line. If the dot is under the water, the ink washes into the tumbler.
items.art: A simple drawing of a paper strip clipped to a pencil across a tumbler, its end in water, with a dot on a line near the bottom, and five empty label boxes.

items.p: Most green sketch pens are a mixture of two dyes. Draw what a green dot might look like after the water has climbed the strip. Colour and label each band.
items.a: A strip with a pencil line at the bottom, a band of one colour, such as blue, and a band of another colour, such as yellow, above or below it.
items.why: Many green sketch pens split into a yellow dye and a blue dye. Which one goes higher depends on the pen. A strong drawing shows two separate bands, both above the pencil line.
items.art: A blank paper strip outline with a pencil line near the bottom.

items.p: Your black sketch pen dot turned into blue and purple bands. Explain why, in two or three sentences.
items.a: The black ink was a mixture of a blue dye and a purple dye. The water dissolved them and carried them up the paper. Each dye travelled a different distance, so they came apart.
items.why: A strong answer says the colours were in the ink all along, and that each dye travels its own distance.

items.p: Arjun puts four dots on one strip: a black sketch pen, a green sketch pen, a ballpoint pen and a brown sketch pen. Which dot will most likely stay where it is?
items.why: Ballpoint ink does not dissolve in water, so the water cannot carry it. Sketch pen inks dissolve in water and move up the strip.

items.p: If two black inks look exactly the same, they must be the same mixture of dyes.
items.why: False. Different pen makers mix different dyes to make black. Two inks can look the same and still split into different colours on a wet strip.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: two or more substances mixed but not joined
a coloured substance that dissolves in a liquid
to break into pieces too small to see and spread through a liquid
the pattern of bands left on the paper
what you saw or measured that shows whether an idea is true
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These words come up all through the unit. A strong answer could also give an example of each.

items.p: Two friends in Mysuru look at a black sketch pen dot that has split into blue and purple.

views.says: The ink is black. I can see that it's black when I write with it.
The ink is really blue and purple. The black is just a trick.

items.ask: Who do you agree with more? Use what you saw in the Which Pen test. Then say one thing the other friend has right.
items.a: A strong answer sees that both have part of it. The ink is a mixture of blue and purple dyes, as the strip shows. Lakshmi is right that the mixture looks black. Farhan is right that blue and purple are in it. The black is not a trick: it is how the dyes look together.
items.why: This question asks the child to use evidence and to see that 'looks black' and 'is made of blue and purple dyes' can both be true.

items.p: Rasam boils over onto the gas flame, and the blue flame turns yellow-orange for a moment. What in the rasam makes that colour?
items.why: Salt has sodium in it, and sodium makes a flame yellow-orange. Water alone does not change the flame much. A taste is not a substance that gives a colour.

items.p: On your strip, one pen's dot did not move at all, even when the water went past it. What can you say about that ink?
items.a: The ink does not dissolve in water, so the water cannot carry it up the strip. It might be a ballpoint or a permanent marker. To separate it, you would need a different liquid.
items.why: A strong answer explains the result, instead of saying the test failed. A dot that does not move is a clue too.

items.p: Three of these are mixtures. Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: Salt is one substance: sodium joined to chlorine. Air is a mixture of gases, seawater is water with salt and other substances in it, and rasam is many things mixed together.

items.p: In the Which Pen test, the water climbed 10 cm and a blue dye went 5 cm, half the way. Divya runs the same pen on a strip where the water climbs 20 cm. About how far will the blue dye go?
items.why: With the same paper and water, a dye travels about the same share of the way. Half of 20 cm is 10 cm. Picking 5 cm forgets that the water went further. Picking 20 cm means thinking the dye keeps up with the water.

items.p: In the Which Pen test, why must every dot be the same size and on the same pencil line?
items.a: So the test is fair. If one dot is bigger or starts higher, its bands could look different because of that, not because of the ink. Then we could not tell which pen matched.
items.why: A strong answer says that only the pen should change, so any difference comes from the ink.

items.p: In the story, the secret note's strip matched Arun's pen. Two cousins argue about what this proves.

views.says: It proves Arun wrote the note. His pen matched.
It proves nothing. Anyone could have used any pen.

items.ask: Who is closer to the truth? Say what the strip does show, and what it does not show. Then say one thing the other cousin has right.
items.a: A strong answer says the strip shows which ink wrote the note: Arun's pen. It does not show who held the pen. Divya is right that the evidence points at Arun's pen. Arjun is right that a pen can be used by anyone, so more questions are needed. But the test does tell us something, so it does not prove nothing.
items.why: Real forensic scientists are careful in the same way: evidence answers one question, not every question.

items.p: Sodium's yellow-orange colour is so strong that it can hide the colours of other elements in a flame.
items.why: True. Even a tiny trace of sodium gives a bright yellow-orange. Chemists who test for other elements have to keep everything very clean, or the sodium colour hides the rest.

items.p: Match each element to the colour it gives a flame.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each element gives its own colours. Firework makers use strontium for red and copper for blue, for example.

items.p: Put these events in the order they happened.
items: Bunsen and Kirchhoff find a new sky-blue element, caesium
Auguste Comte writes that we will never know what stars are made of
Bunsen and Kirchhoff find that each element gives its own set of coloured lines
Bunsen's new burner gives an almost colourless flame
a: Auguste Comte writes that we will never know what stars are made of
Bunsen's new burner gives an almost colourless flame
Bunsen and Kirchhoff find that each element gives its own set of coloured lines
Bunsen and Kirchhoff find a new sky-blue element, caesium
items.why: Comte wrote in 1835. Bunsen's burner came in 1855. The coloured lines were found in 1859, and caesium in 1860. A strong answer sees that the burner had to come first, so the colours could be seen clearly.

items.p: Draw the flame in the flame test for each of the three cups: plain water, sugar water and salt water. Colour each flame and label it.
items.a: Three flames: a blue flame for plain water, perhaps with a tiny orange spark, a blue flame for sugar water, and a bright yellow-orange flame for salt water.
items.why: Only the salt water has much sodium, so only it turns the flame bright yellow-orange. A strong drawing labels which flame is which.
items.art: Three blank flame outlines above three cups labelled plain water, sugar water and salt water.

items.p: In the flame test, the grown-up uses a clean spoon for each cup. Why?
opts: So no salt from one cup is carried into the next test
So the spoons don't get scratched
items.why: Even a trace of salt left on a spoon can make a flame flash yellow-orange. A clean spoon for each cup makes the test fair.

items.p: An element is a substance made of only one kind of ____.
a: atom
items.why: Sodium is made only of sodium atoms. Salt is not an element, because it is made of sodium atoms and chlorine atoms joined together.

items.p: Salt water and sugar water look exactly the same. Explain how a flame can tell them apart.
items.a: Salt has sodium in it. When salt water is heated in a flame, the sodium gives out yellow-orange light. Sugar has no sodium, so sugar water does not make that colour.
items.why: A strong answer names sodium and says that each element gives its own colour.

items.p: Sort these inks and colours: will a dot of each one move up a wet paper strip?
items.a: see items
items.why: Inks made with dyes that dissolve in water move up the strip. Ballpoint ink, permanent marker ink and the carbon in Indian ink do not dissolve in water, so they stay put.

items.p: In the flame test, even the plain tap water gave two or three tiny orange sparks. Why?
opts: Tap water has a little salt dissolved in it
The spoon was made of gold
items.why: Tap water has small amounts of dissolved salts, including a little sodium. So it gives a few sparks, but far fewer than salt water. This is why chemists ask 'how pure?'.

items.p: Here is a drawing of a dried strip from the Which Pen test. Label the parts.
a: The pencil line is near the bottom.
Where the dot started is on the pencil line.
The blue band is the highest colour.
The purple band is between the start and the blue band.
How far the water reached is a pencil mark near the top.
items.why: A strong answer sees that every colour started on the pencil line, and that no colour went further than the water.
items.art: A dried strip drawing with a line near the bottom, a faint dot on it, a purple band above, a blue band higher up and a pencil mark near the top, with five empty label boxes.

items.p: Three of these are elements. Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: Salt is not an element. It is sodium and chlorine joined together. Sodium, copper and oxygen are each made of one kind of atom.

items.p: Your friend says, 'My strip tells me the names of the dyes in my pen.' What does the strip really show? What would a chemist do to name a dye?
items.a: The strip shows how many dyes there are, their colours, and how far each one went. It does not give their names. A chemist would run a dye whose name is known beside it on the same paper, and see if they match, or do more tests.
items.why: A strong answer separates what the evidence shows from what it does not, and suggests comparing with a known dye.

items.p: Lakshmi has a bottle of green food colour. Design a test to find out whether it is one dye or a mixture. Say what you would use, what you would do, and what each result would mean.
items.a: Use a strip of kitchen towel, a pencil line 2 cm from the bottom, one small drop of food colour on the line, and a tumbler with 1 cm of water. Hang the strip so the end dips in. If the green stays as one band, it is probably one dye. If it splits into yellow and blue bands, it is a mixture.
items.why: A strong answer names the materials, the steps and what each result would show. An even stronger one runs a yellow and a blue food colour beside it to compare.

items.p: Two real people disagreed about the stars. Auguste Comte wrote in 1835. Gustav Kirchhoff did his tests in 1859.

views.says: We can measure where stars are and how they move. But we will never know what they are made of, because we can never go there.
Light carries a pattern for each element that gave it out. If we read the pattern in starlight, we know what the star is made of.

items.ask: In 1835, before any tests, whose side would you have taken, and why? Then say what changed in 1859. Is there anything about Comte's thinking that was sensible?
items.a: A strong answer sees that Comte's view was sensible with what people knew in 1835: nobody could go to a star or test a piece of one. What changed was new evidence. Kirchhoff and Bunsen found that each element's light has its own pattern, and matched sodium's pattern in sunlight. So you do not have to go somewhere to test what it is made of.
items.why: This question shows that a wise person can be wrong when new evidence has not been found yet.

items.p: Two black pens give exactly the same bands on kitchen towel in water. What should a chemist do next?
opts: Decide they are the same ink
Try another test, such as a different paper or a different liquid
items.why: One matching test is good evidence, but two different inks could still behave alike on one paper. A different paper or liquid may separate them. Chemists use more than one test before they are sure.

items.p: A test that shows which pen wrote a note also shows who wrote it.
items.why: False. The strip shows which ink was used. Anyone could have held the pen. In the story, the strip matched Arun's pen, but Ammamma had borrowed it.

items.p: Predict: you put a yellow dot and a blue dot on top of each other on one strip, and run it. Draw what you expect. Then draw what a green sketch pen strip looked like, if you tested one. Are they alike?
items.a: Two strips. The yellow and blue mix splits into a yellow band and a blue band. The green strip may show the same two colours.
items.why: If a green ink gives the same bands as yellow plus blue, that is strong evidence that the green is a mixture of a yellow dye and a blue dye.
items.art: Two blank strips side by side, each with a pencil line near the bottom.

items.p: In 1868, astronomers saw a yellow line in the Sun's light that no known element gave. Why did they decide it was a new element?
opts: Every known element had been tested, and none gave a line in that exact place
items.why: Each element gives lines in its own exact places. A line that matched no known element had to come from an unknown one. It was named helium, and found on Earth in 1895.

items.p: The Greek words inside 'chromatography' mean ____ writing.
a: colour
items.why: 'Chroma' means colour and 'graphein' means to write. Mikhail Tsvet chose the name because his first separations were of coloured substances in leaves.

items.p: Sort these tests. Does each one separate a mixture, or show which element is in something?
items: a magnet over iron filings and sand
items.a: see items
items.why: Paper strips, chalk columns, sieves and magnets pull the parts of a mixture apart. Flame colours and split starlight show which elements are present, from their light.

items.p: Put the steps of a fair flame test in order.
items: Look at the flame's colour before testing anything
Cool the spoon and use a clean one for the next cup
Dip a clean spoon in the first cup
Hold the wet spoon in the edge of the flame for 5 seconds
a: Look at the flame's colour before testing anything
Dip a clean spoon in the first cup
Hold the wet spoon in the edge of the flame for 5 seconds
Write down the colour
Cool the spoon and use a clean one for the next cup
items.why: You need the flame's normal colour first, to compare with. A clean spoon each time stops one cup's salt spoiling the next test.

items.p: Mikhail Tsvet poured leaf colour through a glass tube packed with chalk powder. Explain how his chalk tube and your paper strip work in the same way.
items.a: In both, a liquid moves through something with tiny gaps, chalk powder or paper fibres. The liquid carries the substances in the mixture, and the chalk or paper holds them back. Each substance moves at its own speed, so they separate into bands.
items.why: A strong answer names both parts: the moving liquid and the material that holds the substances back.

items.p: Robert Bunsen made a gas burner whose flame is almost colourless. Why did that help him study flame colours?
opts: The colours of the substances showed clearly, without the flame's own colour in the way
items.why: A candle flame is already bright yellow, so a yellow from sodium would be hard to see. In an almost colourless flame, each substance's colour stands out.

items.p: Here is a drawing of the flame test. Label the parts.
a: The blue gas flame is on the burner.
The wet steel spoon is held in the edge of the flame.
The yellow-orange flash is around the spoon.
The cloth is in the grown-up's hand, around the spoon's end.
The child stands one metre away.
items.why: A strong answer shows the safety parts too: the cloth and the child standing back.
items.art: A drawing of a gas burner with a flame, a grown-up's hand holding a spoon in it with a cloth, an orange flash, and a child standing back, with five empty label boxes.

items.p: Match each job to the chemist's test it uses.
pairs: A food lab checks chilli powder for colours that are not allowed
A firework maker wants a red firework
adding an element that gives a red flame
An astronomer finds out what a star is made of
reading the lines in its light
A forensic scientist checks whether a word was added to a cheque
A chemist checks a white powder for sodium
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Chromatography separates mixtures, and light shows which elements are present. A strong answer could say why each test fits its job.

items.p: A spoon of plain tap water gave tiny orange sparks in the flame. Use this to explain why chemists say almost nothing is perfectly pure.
items.a: Tap water looks pure, but the orange sparks show it has a little sodium in it, from dissolved salts. Most things have small traces of other substances in them. Better tests find smaller and smaller traces, so chemists ask how pure something is, not whether it is pure.
items.why: A strong answer uses the sparks as evidence and links them to traces of other substances.

items.p: Black ink looked like one thing, but water showed it was several dyes. Can you think of something else that looks like one thing but is really a mixture? How could you test it?
items.a: For example, air looks like nothing, but it is a mixture of gases. Seawater looks like water, but it has salt in it: let some dry in a plate in the sun and salt is left. Rasam looks like one liquid, but it is many things.
items.why: A strong answer gives an example and a real way to test it, such as drying, sieving or a flame test.

applications: Food safety labs use chromatography to check spices, sweets and oils for colours and substances that are not allowed.
Hospital labs separate the substances in blood and urine to check a person's health and the medicines in their body.
Sports labs test athletes for banned medicines with chromatography.
Forensic scientists compare the inks on letters, cheques and wills to find out whether words were added later.
Water labs test drinking water for harmful substances, such as pesticides, with chromatography.
Medicine factories check that every batch of tablets is pure enough.
Firework makers, such as those in Sivakasi in Tamil Nadu, colour their sparks with elements: strontium for red, barium for green, copper for blue and sodium for yellow.
Old orange street lights glow with sodium's yellow-orange light.
Astronomers read the light of stars and planets to find out what they are made of.
Chemists use a method called Raman spectroscopy, named after C.V. Raman, to identify substances from the light they scatter. Raman found the effect in Kolkata in 1928.

open_questions.q: How many different substances are there in one living cell?
open_questions.why_open: Labs have found thousands, but some are present in amounts too small for today's tests. Nobody has a complete list for any cell.

open_questions.q: Can we find signs of life on a planet around another star, from the light that passes through its air?
open_questions.why_open: Telescopes can now read the air of a few far planets. Scientists look for gases that living things make. No clear sign of life has been found yet, and some claims are still argued about.

open_questions.q: What is dark matter made of?
open_questions.why_open: Most of the matter in the universe gives out no light at all, so chemists' light tests cannot read it. Nobody knows what it is.

open_questions.q: Could a machine ever find substances as well as a sniffer dog's nose?
open_questions.why_open: Sniffer dogs can find tiny traces of explosives and drugs. Engineers are building 'electronic noses', but none yet matches a trained dog everywhere.

open_questions.q: Are there more elements still to be found?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have made elements up to number 118 in labs. Heavier ones may exist for a tiny moment, and teams are trying to make them.

maths.problem: On one strip, the water climbed 10 cm. The blue dye went 8 cm and the purple dye went 3 cm. How much further did the blue dye travel than the purple?
maths.explain: The blue went 8 cm and the purple went 3 cm. 8 take away 3 is 5. So the blue travelled 5 cm further.
maths.context: This is about the Which Pen test, where water climbs a paper strip and carries each dye in an ink its own distance.
maths.why_maths: The gap between two bands tells you how differently two dyes behave. Taking one height from the other shows it.

maths.problem: On a strip where the water climbed 10 cm, a yellow dye went 5 cm, half of the way. On a longer strip, the water climbs 16 cm. Where would you expect the yellow dye to stop?
maths.explain: The yellow dye went half the way on the first strip. With the same paper and water, it goes about half the way again. Half of 16 cm is 8 cm.
maths.context: This is about the Which Pen test. With the same paper and water, each dye travels about the same share of the way the water goes.
maths.why_maths: Chemists compare dyes by the share of the way they travel, not by centimetres, because strips are not all the same length. A fraction does that.

maths.problem: In the Does Every Colour Split test, the black pen had 3 dyes, brown had 4, green had 2, purple had 2, orange had 2 and yellow had 1. How many of the six pens were mixtures? Which colour was most likely just one dye?
maths.answer: 5 pens were mixtures. Yellow was most likely one dye.
maths.explain: A mixture has more than one dye. Black, brown, green, purple and orange each had 2 or more, so that is 5 pens. Yellow showed only 1 band, so it is most likely one dye.
maths.context: This is about the Does Every Colour Split test, where you run six sketch pen colours on strips and count the bands.

maths.problem: Auguste Comte wrote in 1835 that we would never know what stars are made of. Kirchhoff showed there was sodium in the Sun in 1859. How many years later was that?
maths.explain: Take the earlier year from the later year. 1859 take away 1835 is 24. Check: 1835 + 24 = 1859.
maths.context: This is about how people found out what the Sun is made of, using flame colours.
maths.why_maths: Working out the gap between two dates shows how quickly a 'never' can be proved wrong once there is a new test.

maths.problem: Each set of strips takes about 8 minutes for the water to climb. You have three tumblers and want to run 12 strips, 2 in each tumbler at a time. How many rounds do you need, and how long will it take?
maths.explain: Three tumblers with 2 strips each hold 6 strips at a time. 12 strips need 2 rounds of 6. 2 rounds of 8 minutes is 16 minutes.
maths.context: This is about the home ink library, where you run a strip for every pen in your home.
maths.why_maths: Planning a test before you start saves time. Equal groups tell you how many rounds you need.

roots.context: We have pulled ink apart with water and seen salt colour a flame. Now we ask what these tests tell us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Two black pens looked exactly alike. On wet paper, each black ink spread into its own set of colours. Each black was a mix of dyes, and water carried each dye its own distance. So things that look the same can be made of different things, and a test can show which.
deep_truth.habit: We decide what a thing is by how it looks: black ink is black ink, and a white powder is a white powder. Looks only show the surface. What a thing is made of shows up in how it behaves when we test it.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Which Pen test, black pens that looked the same on paper gave different bands on the wet strips, and the secret letter matched only one of them. In the flame test, salt water and sugar water looked the same, but only the salt water turned the flame yellow-orange.

three.who_am_i: Your body is a mixture of thousands of substances. Doctors find out which ones, and how much, by testing a little of your blood.
three.what_is_life: Plants make many coloured substances of their own: green ones to catch sunlight, and yellow, orange and red ones too. Chromatography was first used to separate them.
three.what_is_this_world: The Sun, the stars and the Earth are made of the same elements. We know because their light shows the same colours as the elements in our labs.

roots.thread: Black ink looks like one thing, yet water shows it is several dyes. Each dye is made of atoms of a few elements. Every element is built from the same few kinds of tiny particle. Going inwards, many things turn out to be made of fewer and fewer kinds. Going outwards, the same 118 elements make a pen, a flame, your body and the Sun.

teachings.source: Nyaya Sutra 1.1.3 and 1.1.6, by Gautama (also called Akshapada), an Indian book on how we know
teachings.teaching: There are four ways of knowing: seeing for yourself, working it out from signs, comparing with something already known, and the word of a trustworthy person. Comparing means knowing a new thing by its likeness to a thing you know well.
teachings.link: In the Which Pen test you used two of these. You worked out from signs, the coloured bands, which pen was used. You compared the secret strip with strips whose pens you already knew.
The blue and purple in black ink, and the sodium in clear salt water, could not be seen. A test made them show themselves.

science.text: Every element gives out its own exact set of colours of light. The same elements are found on Earth, in the Sun and in far-away stars.
Nobody yet has a complete list of every substance in a single living cell. Some are there in amounts too small for today's tests.

other_view.view: Tests tell us what a thing is made of, and that is all they tell us. Knowing the dyes in an ink is useful, but it carries no lesson about how to see the world. Reading more into it is our choice, not the ink's.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if at home today, with the materials listed. Kitchen towel was chosen over coffee filters, which few Indian homes have, with blotting paper from a stationery shop as the better option and a folded paper napkin as a back-up. The Which Pen test asks for black pens from two different makers, because two pens from the same packet give the same pattern. It says what to do if every black stays black, and treats a permanent marker that does not move as a useful result. Strips hang two to a tumbler from a pencil and clips, so they do not touch each other or the sides. Water on kitchen towel climbs 8 to 10 cm in about 5 to 10 minutes, so the timings allow for that. The flame test uses a wet steel spoon held by a grown-up, not salt sprinkled on the burner, and needs a gas stove. Homes with induction cooktops have no flame, so they watch the Periodic Videos flame video instead, and the flame test is outside the spine. The three powders activity uses no tasting, and only the grown-up heats. The spine is One Dot, the Which Pen test, the explanation cards, roots and the quiz: about 85 minutes, all doable in a city flat with sketch pens, kitchen towel, a tumbler and water.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out what the Sun is made of, when nobody can go there? This card tells the true story.
how_we_found_out.story: In 1835, the French philosopher Auguste Comte wrote about the stars. We can measure their shapes, distances and movements, he said, but we will never know what they are made of. It seemed obvious. Nobody can travel to a star. In Heidelberg, in Germany, the chemist Robert Bunsen was studying the colours that substances give to a flame. His new gas burner made a hot flame that was almost colourless, so each colour showed clearly. But some colours looked alike. His friend Gustav Kirchhoff, a physicist, suggested splitting the light with a prism. In 1859 they found that each element gave its own set of thin coloured lines. Sodium always gave two yellow lines, close together. Sunlight split by a prism has thin dark lines in it, and two of them sat exactly where sodium's yellow lines were. Kirchhoff shone sunlight through a flame with sodium in it, and those dark lines grew darker. Sodium takes in the same colour it gives out. So there is sodium in the Sun. In 1860, the two men saw new blue lines in spring water. They had found a new element, and named it caesium, from a Latin word for sky blue. Comte had died two years before he was shown to be wrong.
how_we_found_out.who: Robert Bunsen, a German chemist, and Gustav Kirchhoff, a German physicist, proving Auguste Comte, a French philosopher, wrong
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: We can never know what the stars are made of, because we cannot go there. Bunsen and Kirchhoff showed that each element's light has its own pattern, and found sodium's pattern in sunlight.
